newsitem.title: USA: Energy, grain prices lead commodities lower.
newsitem.headline: Energy, grain prices lead commodities lower.

text.p: Oil and grain prices fell Friday as traders took profits on this week's gains and as optimism about supplies increased.
The selling pressured many markets, with the Knight Ridder Commodity Research Bureau index of 17 commodity futures ending down 0.51 point at 245.70.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange oil prices, were led lower by heating oil despite colder weather in the Northeast, which would increase demand in the world's largest market for the fuel.

Countering that was news that Colonial Pipeline Co., which operates a primary Houston-to-New York conduit for fuels, had extended pipeline space allocations through January due to heavy competition to ship heating oil northward.
"The Colonial allocation kept the pressure on heating oil despite colder weather in the East Coast," said Tom Bentz, analyst with ING Derivatives in New York.
Heating oil for January delivery lost 0.81 cent to settle at 72.97 cents a gallon, and January gasoline fell 1.03 cents to 70.19 cents a gallon.

Worries about heating oil supplies were also eased by news that about 120,000 metric tons (870,000 barrels) of Russian heating oil was due to arrive in the United States in the next week, in addition to a previously reported 60,000 tons (435,000 barrels).
Crude oil prices also fell, with February crude down 37 cents a barrel at $25.08 in sympathy with heating oil and on bearish supply news of its own, traders said.

Saudi Arabia's deputy oil minister, Abdel Aziz bin Salman, said Friday the Saudis, the world's biggest producers of oil, might not need to cut oil production if the United Nations lifted sanctions against Iraq.

Iraq recently resumed limited exports of oil under a U.N. deal allowing it to sell $2 billion worth of oil for food over six months. But diplomatic sources said broad sanctions against Iraq were unlikely to be lifted for years, or at least until Iraqi President Saddam Hussein was out of power.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, wheat futures closed lower on improved weather in that country's wheat-growing regions. The Argentine crop has been hurt this year by torrential rains.
March wheat ended at $3.93-1/4 per bushel, down 7 cents.
Reports of near-ideal growing weather in Brazil also hurt soybean prices. January soybean futures closed 5-3/4 cents a bushel lower at $7.02.
"Plantings are almost completed and the crop is off to a good start," Ron Kucha of O'Connor and Co. said of the soybean crop in Brazil, the No. 2 exporter after the United States.
Corn futures closed mixed, with the March contract closing 3/4 cent a bushel higher at $2.66-3/4.
Traders said cash market demand tied to healthy exports and livestock feed demand due to low Midwest temperatures were supporting prices.

At the New York Cotton Exchange, frozen orange juice prices fell to new life-of-contract lows as traders bet that low temperatures would not pose a threat to the big Florida citrus crop. March futures closed down 0.95 cent at 90.70 cents a pound.
According to meteorologists, low temperatures in Florida will reach between 44 and 34 degrees Fahrenheit over the weekend, not low enough to cause a freeze.
